papers.what_it_is: A Fujitsu Research paper that proposes a quantum-circuit Transformer (MQT) to estimate molecular ground-state energies and tests it numerically on four small molecules.

assertions.value: The authors report that MQT performs comparably to the classical Transformer for H2 and reduces the average estimation error by 42% in LiH, 18% in BeH2 and 74% in H4.
assertions.anchor: Results, estimating potential energy curves, Fig. 3 and Tab. I discussion
quotes: These results suggest that MQT performs comparably to the classical Transformer for H2 but outperforms it for other molecules, reducing the average estimation error by 42% in LiH, 18% in BeH2, and 74% in H4 compared to the classical Transformer.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study of four small molecules.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against a classical Transformer of the same model dimensionality, not against a tuned classical chemistry method.

assertions.value: The authors report that pretraining on other molecules reduced the LiH few-shot error by nearly 19% and gave an 11% improvement over the neural-network meta-VQE method; the conclusion calls the gain modest.
assertions.anchor: Results, estimating the potential energy curve with pretraining, and Discussion; Fig. 5
quotes: The pretrained model yields more accurate estimations in few-shot learning compared to only using fine-tuning, as indicated by reducing nearly 19% of error to the theoretical values
Notably, with the same number of training data points, our model achieves an 11% improvement in few-shot learning performance compared to the neural network-based meta-VQE [24]
Results showed that pretraining modestly improved accuracy for the LiH potential energy curve compared to an untrained model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the paper itself calls the improvement modest.

assertions.value: The authors state that scaling MQT is limited by amplitude embedding of the output state, whose state preparation complexity scales exponentially with the number of qubits, and that classical preparation of the state vector needs memory that grows exponentially.
quotes: where direct state preparation is challenging due to the complexity scaling exponentially with the number of qubits nq.
Even with efficient qRAM, preparing the state vector on a classical computer prior to amplitude embedding demands memory that grows exponentially with nq, hindering scalability.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scaling limit in the Discussion section.

assertions.value: The authors state that MQT was tested on the molecules H2, LiH, BeH2 and H4, with qubit counts from 8 to 14 and fermion-to-qubit mappings as given in the quote.
quotes: we employ the Bravyi-Kitaev mapping for H2 (8 qubits), LiH (12 qubits), and BeH2 (14 qubits), and the Jordan-Wigner transformation for H4 (8 qubits).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, numerical experiments section.
assertions.reader_inference: Every test molecule is small (at most 14 qubits), so the result says nothing about larger molecules.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-inspired Embeddings Projection and Similarity Metrics for Representation Learning
papers.what_it_is: A quantum-inspired projection head (low-entanglement circuit simulation) that compresses BERT embeddings, compared with a classical fully connected head on TREC 2019 and 2020 passage ranking.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum-inspired projection head gives competitive performance on passage ranking with 32 times fewer parameters than the classical fully connected head.
quotes: Empirical evaluations showed that our approach delivers competitive performance on passageranking tasks with 32 times fewer parameters than its classical pendant.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on two benchmarks.
assertions.reader_inference: The method is quantum-inspired and runs on classical hardware, so it is evidence about classical ML, not about quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the BERTbase backbone, the quantum-inspired model beat the classical model by about 1 point at the full dataset (100%) and by over 2.6 points at the smallest dataset (1%).
assertions.anchor: Section 6, training dataset size, Fig. 5 and Table C4
quotes: the quantum-inspired model (QBEC) outperforms the classical model (BEC) when utilizing the BERTbase backbone, which has not been pre-trained on sentence representations.

For instance, while the performance gap between BEC and QBEC is approximately 1 point for the full dataset (100%), this gap widens significantly to over 2.6 points for the smallest dataset (1%) on both benchmarks (Table C4).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the backbone had not been trained on sentence representations.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage appears where the baseline backbone was untrained for the task, so it may not carry over to a well-tuned backbone.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the fine-tuned BERTv5 backbone the quantum-inspired head scored -0.23% on TREC19 and +0.85% on TREC20 relative to the classical head.
assertions.anchor: Section 6, quantum-inspired vs classical compression models, p.16
quotes: the quantum-inspired approach (QBEC) demonstrates a slight performance decrease (-0.23%) on TREC19, while achieving a more substantial performance increase (+0.85%) on TREC20 when the fine-tuned model BERTv5 is employed as the backbone.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; the sign differs between the two benchmarks.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is mixed across benchmarks when the backbone is already trained.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains uncertain whether the observed performance can be ascribed solely to the compression head.
quotes: Nonetheless, it remains uncertain whether these performances obtained can be ascribed solely to the compression head.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, Section 6, p.16.

papers.title_in_file: Double descent in quantum kernel methods
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections II to VIII (theorems, experiments, discussion); appendix proofs only skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper showing that linear regression in quantum feature spaces and quantum kernel methods can show a double-descent test-error peak.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for a Lipschitz continuous quantum feature map with p linearly independent dimensions and i.i.d. Gaussian inputs, the test error of the linear model peaks with high probability at N = p for large enough N and p.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Theorem 1 (appendix has the formal statement)
quotes: peaks with high probability at N = p, for large enough N and p.
Theorem 1 suggests that in the asymptotic limit, one might observe the phenomenon of double descent in quantum kernel methods if the data distribution is suitably aligned.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, Section IV, with proof in the appendix; it holds only asymptotically and for Gaussian inputs.

assertions.value: The paper proves that for a quantum kernel model built on the reduced-density-matrix projection of a Lipschitz continuous feature map on n qubits with i.i.d. Gaussian training samples, the training set size at which the test error peaks is, with high probability, linear in the number of qubits.
quotes: the training set size N at which the peak in test error occurs with high probability is linear in the number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Corollary 3, Section VII, with its proof given in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical experiments on quantum kernel methods with real-world datasets and several system sizes confirm a test error peak, and they note that the practical benefit depends on a deeper second dip in test error.
quotes: our numerical experiments on quantum kernel methods across different real-world datasets and system sizes further confirm the existence of a test error peak, a characteristic feature of double descent.
Although this work focuses on the peak, the practical benefit hinges on achieving a deeper second dip in test error.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from numerical experiments; the paper does not show that the second dip beats a simpler model.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper shows the peak, not that the overparameterized regime gives better learning than classical models.

assertions.value: The authors state that their work does not solve concentration in quantum kernels, and that adapting the double descent framework to parameterized quantum circuits needs further investigation and is left for future work.
quotes: Our work does not solve concentration. Indeed, exponentially concentrated kernels with flat spectra will yield poor generalization in practice regardless.
Thus, further investigation is required to adapt the double descent framework to PQCs, a direction we leave for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limits, Section VIII.

papers.title_in_file: Geometric spectral theory of quantum graphs
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and a search of the full text for quantum computing and machine learning (no hits); the later chapters on eigenvalue estimates were not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: Lecture notes on how the spectrum of a Schroedinger-type operator on a metric graph depends on the graph geometry.
papers.why_not: Quantum graphs here are differential operators on metric graphs in mathematical physics. The notes do not discuss quantum computing or machine learning.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, thesis overview, Chapter 4 introduction, theorem statements and discussion, Chapter 2 and 3 summaries; the proofs and appendices were not read line by line.
papers.what_it_is: An MIT PhD thesis that represents stabilizer codes as graphs and uses them for code construction, encoding circuits and decoding.

assertions.value: The thesis proves that every stabilizer code is essentially uniquely represented by an encoder-respecting graph, and conversely, with an efficient compilation algorithm between tableaus and graphs.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Chapter 4, Theorem 4.1.1 (informal), precise forms in Sections 4.2 and 4.4
quotes: Every stabilizer code is essentially uniquely represented by an encoder-respecting graph satisfying some rules, and conversely every such graph essentially uniquely represents a stabilizer code.
We prove that this graph representation is in bijection with tableaus and give an efficient compilation algorithm that transforms tableaus into graphs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.1.1 and Theorem 4.2.5, Chapter 4.

assertions.value: The thesis states, as a theorem, that an efficient algorithm produces an encoding circuit whose depth is bounded, up to a small additive constant, by twice the maximum degree of the graph.
quotes: (3) There exists an efficient algorithm which produces an encoding circuit for C(G) whose depth is bounded by (up to a small additive constant) twice the maximum degree of G.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.1.2 item 3, Chapter 4 (informal statement; formal version in Section 4.4).

assertions.value: The thesis states that randomly connecting edges of its graphs gives a large class of codes in which almost all members satisfy a trade-off between rate, distance and stabilizer weight, extending the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov result, which has always large stabilizer weight.
quotes: By randomly connecting edges of our graphs, we give a large class of codes for which almost all members satisfy a trade-off between rate, distance, and stabilizer weight.

This extends the result of the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov bound, which shows by a coarsegrained probabilistic stabilizer tableau analysis a similar result with a rate-distance trade-off but always large stabilizer weight.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 4.1.6 and Theorem 4.5.10, Chapter 4.

assertions.value: The thesis states that the generality of its results carries limitations that do not exist for highly specific qLDPC constructions, and that it does not aim at asymptotically good qLDPC codes.
quotes: The universality of these results therefore has limitations that do not exist for highly specific quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) constructions.
Thus, our intention is not to use the graph representation as a means for continued study into asymptotically good qLDPC codes with very large constants
assertions.certainty_reason: The thesis states its own scope and limits in Chapter 4, Section 4.1.1.

papers.title_in_file: Bringing Quantum Algorithms to Automated Machine Learning: A Systematic Review of AutoML Frameworks Regarding Extensibility for QML Algorithms
papers.what_it_is: A review that selects open-source AutoML frameworks for later extension with quantum machine learning algorithms, using four industrial use-case studies and expert interviews.

assertions.value: The authors report selecting Ray as the low-level and AutoGluon as the high-level AutoML framework, because they fulfilled all requirements and received the best evaluation feedback in the use-case study.
quotes: Finally, we select Ray and AutoGluon as the suitable low- and high-level frameworks respectively, as they fulfil all requirements sufficiently and received the best evaluation feedback during the use-case study.
assertions.certainty_reason: An outcome of one multi-criteria selection with interview-based feedback.
assertions.reader_inference: The selection rests on classical AutoML use-cases; no QML algorithm was run in these frameworks.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study used four use-cases covering classification, regression and forecasting on tabular, time series and image data.
quotes: The types of use-cases belong to the ML domains of classification, regression and forecasting, and work with tabular, time series and image input data.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its study setup, Section 6.

assertions.value: The authors state that, after this assessment, an open-source AutoQML framework combining AutoML and quantum computing will be implemented, and that stand-alone QML algorithms will be developed and integrated later.
quotes: Following this assessment, an open-source AutoQML framework will be implemented that combines AutoML and QC.
For that, stand-alone QML algorithms will be developed which will be later integrated directly or as an independent backend into one of the existing AutoML libraries discussed above.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope, Section 6.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not evaluate any QML algorithm inside an AutoML framework.

assertions.value: The authors state that ML methods for today's quantum hardware must deal with considerable noise along with a limited number of qubits and short circuit depths.
quotes: ML methods for today's quantum hardware have to deal with a considerable amount of noise along with a limited number of qubits and short circuit depths.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement by the authors with no study behind it in this paper.

papers.title_in_file: Learning To Optimize Quantum Neural Network Without Gradients
papers.what_it_is: A gradient-free LSTM meta-optimizer that trains a variational quantum circuit, compared with Adam and gradient descent in simulation.

assertions.value: The paper derives that a gradient-based optimizer needs quadratic time in circuit size per full pass using the parameter-shift rule, while a gradient-free optimizer needs linear time.
assertions.anchor: Section V, Theorem V.1 and the discussion after it
quotes: If A does not require a gradient, then the total time for one full pass takes
The reduction of a quadratic run-time to a linear run-time is significant since this will allow a QNN to scale to a larger number of data points.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem V.1 with proof, Section V; it counts circuit evaluations under the parameter-shift cost model.
assertions.reader_inference: The result compares against parameter-shift gradients and does not include the training cost of the meta-optimizer.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a Gaussian, a spheres and a truncated Iris dataset, the LSTM meta-optimizer found parameters minimizing the cost in far fewer circuit evaluations than the gradient-based optimizers.
quotes: In all cases, the LSTM optimizer is able to find parameters that minimize the cost function in far fewer circuit evaluations than gradient based optimizers.
Experiments on different datasets show that our algorithm has a comparable quality to classical optimization algorithms while significantly outperforming them in terms of computation time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from simulation on three small datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: The datasets are tiny and two-class, so the result does not show the same behavior at scale.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main experiments simulated the optimizers with an infinite number of shots, and that a further experiment used a simulated device with only 100 shots.
quotes: In the experiments on the machine learning datasets we simulated the performance of the optimization algorithms assuming that number of available shots on the device were infinite.
Figure 4 shows the results of our experiments on a simulated quantum device with only 100 shots for measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: All results are simulated; none ran on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that their gradient-free meta-optimization algorithm can potentially scale up to larger dataset sizes in a reasonable amount of time.
quotes: We have proposed a gradient free meta optimization algorithm for quantum neural networks that can potentially scale up to larger dataset sizes in a reasonable amount of time.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim hedged with the word potentially.

papers.title_in_file: Application of Quantum Tensor Networks for Protein Classification
papers.what_it_is: Quantum tensor network models built with the lambeq QNLP library, tested in simulation on binary classification of human protein sequences by subcellular location.

assertions.value: The authors report that their best quantum model reached 94% accuracy, against 0.98 for the ESM2-based classical model.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Section 4, Table 1 and model performance discussion
quotes: Our top-performing quantum model has achieved a 94% accuracy rate, which is comparable to the performance of a classical model that uses the ESM2 protein language model embeddings.
the ESM2-based classical model (Fig. 7), with its high accuracy of 0.98, sets a significant benchmark for performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulated study on one small dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The quantum model is below the classical benchmark. Table 1 shows 0.94 for the best model with discard measurement and 0.83 with postselect.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dataset has 1136 human protein sequences of 80 to 200 amino acids each, classified into two subcellular locations.
quotes: The dataset of human protein sequences has been cleaned and preprocessed to have 80 to 200 amino acids in each sequence.
The dataset is made of 1136 protein sequences after preprocessing
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its dataset, Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum tensor networks were evaluated under idealized conditions without quantum noise, likely giving an optimistic representation of their capabilities.
quotes: The QTNs were evaluated under idealized conditions devoid of quantum noise, likely leading to an optimistic representation of their capabilities.
Such an omission of quantum noise considerations prevents a fully equitable comparison to the classical ESM2 model
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limit, Section 4 Limitations.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their findings underscore a significant advancement over classical models and show the inherent advantages of quantum computing in processing and classifying biological data.
quotes: our findings underscore a significant advancement over classical models, showcasing the inherent advantages of quantum computing in processing and classifying biological data.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper's own results show lower accuracy than the classical ESM2 benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is not supported by the paper's own comparison, which has the quantum model below the classical one (0.94 against 0.98).
